analysis.one_liner: Requires group health plans to cover mental health care on the same terms as physical care.
analysis.headline: The bill received no cosponsors and no vote; it sat on the Senate calendar until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended two federal laws to stop employer group health plans from placing stricter limits on mental health care than on physical care. If a plan charged a high copay for therapy visits but a low one for doctor visits, or capped therapy at 20 visits a year with no cap on physical care, that would no longer be allowed. It did not force any plan to offer mental health benefits in the first place, and it exempted employers with 50 or fewer workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families with job-based health insurance who need mental health care. Today, many plans charge higher copays for therapy, allow fewer visits, and set separate annual and lifetime caps for mental health treatment [S2]. The bill would have required plans that offer mental health coverage to treat it the same way they treat medical and surgical care, including deductibles, coinsurance, copays, and annual and lifetime limits [S3]. People with depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, and other mental illnesses would have gotten care on the same financial terms as anyone getting treatment for a physical illness.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers with job-based insurance needing mental health care

how_it_helps.text: Bars group health plans from imposing treatment limits or cost-sharing on mental health benefits unless comparable limits apply to medical and surgical benefits.
The parity rules cover deductibles, coinsurance, copayments, other cost sharing, and annual and lifetime limits on what a plan will pay.
The bill exempts employers with between 2 and 50 employees, so the rules would bind larger employers only.
It does not preempt stronger state parity laws, so states could keep more protective rules.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and their health insurers, through higher premiums where plans had been limiting mental health coverage more tightly than physical coverage. The bill directed the GAO to study the effects on insurance costs, access, and quality, including the cost of extending parity to substance abuse treatment [S2]. Because plans are not required to offer mental health benefits at all, some plans could have dropped those benefits rather than bring them to parity, shifting costs back onto people who need care [S2].

drawbacks.text: Full parity raises premiums for employers and workers, and the bill's own design required a GAO study of the cost effects before anyone would know how large they were [S2].
The bill does not require any plan to offer mental health benefits; a plan that wanted to avoid parity could drop mental health coverage entirely [S2].
Substance abuse and chemical dependency treatment are explicitly excluded from the parity requirement [S3].
Plans only have to bring in-network mental health benefits to parity; out-of-network mental health care can still be covered on worse terms as long as in-network access is reasonable [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of people with mental illness in job-based plans, equal copays and the removal of separate annual and lifetime caps would have been a substantial gain, and mental health parity drew support across party lines for years before Congress eventually enacted a version in 2008. The real costs are higher premiums, spread across employers and all enrollees, and a design gap: because plans can simply drop mental health benefits, the guarantee is only as strong as a plan's decision to keep offering them. The carve-outs for small employers, substance abuse, and out-of-network care are compromises that leave meaningful gaps, but the core rule is sound.

outcome.mechanism: Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle introduced the bill in November 2003, it was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar, and then nothing happened; no committee took it up, no vote was ever scheduled, and it expired when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005 [S1, S5].

narrative.text: Daschle introduced the bill on November 6, 2003, and it was read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 382 on November 7, 2003.
The only recorded action after placement on the calendar was the sponsor's introductory remarks on May 19, 2004.
No committee is listed for the bill and no floor vote ever occurred; the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers and health insurers were better off, because they never had to bring mental health coverage up to the same terms as physical coverage or absorb the GAO-estimated cost of doing so. People who needed mental health care on job-based plans kept paying higher copays and hitting visit caps and separate limits until Congress passed a broader parity law in 2008.

for.name: Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 6, 2003, and delivered introductory remarks on the floor on May 19, 2004.

against.name: Bill Frist
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote during the 108th Congress; it remained on the Senate calendar until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held and the bill's only listed cosponsor count is zero, so the record shows only the Democratic sponsor and no recorded support or opposition from either party; parity proposals had historically drawn members of both parties.

industries.note: Plans could no longer charge higher copays, allow fewer visits, or set separate annual and lifetime caps for mental health care than for physical care. They could avoid the rules by dropping mental health benefits entirely, and small-group business was exempt.

industries.industry: Large employers offering group health plans
industries.note: Employers with more than 50 workers would face higher premiums if their plans had been limiting mental health coverage more tightly than physical coverage. Employees with mental health needs would gain equal coverage, but the added cost would be spread across the whole workforce.
Removing visit caps and higher cost sharing for therapy and psychiatric care would mean more patients could afford more treatment, expanding demand for mental health services.
